prompt: Read the image file {path}. It is a crop of one column of a printed 1854 Hebrew-English lexicon (Gesenius, Robinson translation). Transcribe every complete printed text line exactly, one array element per printed line, top to bottom. Preserve spelling, capitalisation, punctuation, printed abbreviations, section marks and end-of-line hyphenation. Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Syriac, Greek and Ethiopic must be Unicode text with every visible vowel point, dagesh, accent and diacritic, written in logical order with no bidi control characters; keep the words of a right-to-left phrase in the order they are read, and keep the printed left-to-right order of separate items in a list. Where a page or column header, page number or catchword is present, include it as its own line. If a line is only partially visible at the top or bottom edge, omit it entirely rather than guessing. Never add, reorder, translate, normalise or omit anything that is fully visible. If the crop contains no text, return an empty array.

lines: אדנ
אדר
אֲדֹנָי see after אָדוֹן.
אֲדֹנִי־בֶזֶק (lord of Bezek) Adoni-Be-
zek, name or title of a king of the Ca-
naanitish city Bezek, Judg. 1, 5. 6. 7.
אֲדֹנִי־צֶדֶק (lord of justice) Adoni-
zedek, pr. n. of a Canaanitish king of
Jerusalem, Josh. 10, 1. 3.
אֲדֹנִיָּהוּ (my lord is Jehovah) Adoni-
jah, pr. n. m. a) A son of David, who
attempted to usurp the succession, 1 K.
1, 8 sq. Called also אֲדֹנִיָּה v. 5. 2 Sam.
In Ezra 2, 13 the same person is called
אֲדֹנִיקָם Adonikam, i. e. lord of the ene-
my. Comp. Ezra 8, 13. Neh. 7, 18.
אֲדֹנִיקָם see אֲדֹנִיָּהוּ c.
אֲדֹנִירָם (lord of altitude) Adoniram,
pr. n. of a man who had charge of the
public works under David and Solomon,
1 K. 4, 6. By an unusual contraction,
called אֲדוֹרָם Adoram, 2 Sam. 20, 24.
1 K. 12, 18; also הֲדוֹרָם 2 Chr. 10, 18.
* אָדַר in Kal not used, pr. to be large,
great, ample, see deriv. אֶדֶר, אַדֶּרֶת;
comp. أَدِرَ to have the hernia, pr. to be
swollen; آدَرُ swollen, inflated, e. g.
the belly. Kindr. is הָדַר.—Trop. to be
great, splendid, powerful; see in אַדִּיר.
Niph. to be made great, to be magni-
fied, glorious. Part. Ex. 15, 6 יְמִינְךָ יְהוָֹה
נֶאְדָּרִי בַּכֹּחַ thy right hand, Jehovah, is
magnified in might, is made glorious in
strength. The Yod in נֶאְדָּרִי is para-
gogic.
Hiph. to magnify, to make honourable,
Deriv. אֶדֶר, אַדֶּרֶת, אַדִּיר, and the com-
pounds אַדְרַמֶּלֶךְ, אַדְרַגָּזְרִין.
אֲדָר Adar, the twelſth Hebrew month,
from the new moon of March to that of
April ; or according to the Rabbins,
from the new moon of February to that
17. 19. 21. Gr. Ἀδάρ, 1 Macc. 7, 43. Syr.
ܐܳܕܳܪ, Arab. آذَارُ, أَذَارُ, and آذَارُ, the
sixth month of the Syro-Macedonians.
Perh. from Pers. آذر fire.
אֲדָר Chald. id. Ezra 6, 15.
אַדָּר see חֲצַר־אַדָּר.
אֶדֶר m. pr. largeness, amplitude;
hence
1. a wide cloak, mantle, i. q. אַדֶּרֶת,
2. greatness, splendour, whence Zech.
11, 13 אֶדֶר הַיְקָר splendour of the price,
i. e. the splendid price, ironically.
אִדַּר Chald. (r. נָדַר II) area, threshing-
floor, pr. a wide open place, Dan. 2, 35.
Syr. ܐܶܕܪܳܐ, Arab. أَنْدَرٌ. Hence some
refer it to Arab. ندر excidit granum;
but in Arab. اندر the nd seems to be
for dd.
אֲדַרְגָּזְרִין Chald. plur. m. chief-judges,
Dan. 3, 2. 3. Compounded from אֲדַר i. q.
אֶדֶר greatness, comp. אַדִּיר no. 3; and
גָּזְרִין judges, comp. גְּזַר .
אַדְרַזְדָּא Chald. adv. Ezra 7, 2. 3 right-
ly, diligently, carefully, Vulg. diligenter.
Prob. it is a Persian word, perh. i. q. Pers.
دُرُسْت recte, vere, probe.
אֲדַרְכּוֹן m. only in Plur. אֲדַרְכֹּנִים
1 Chr. 29, 7. Ezra 8, 27, i. q. דַּרְכְּמוֹן, a
daric, a Persian coin of pure gold, com-
mon also among the Jews while they
were under the Persian dominion. The
א is prosthetic; comp. in Mishna דַּרְכּוֹן
and Syr. ܕܰܪܺܝܟܽܘܢܳܐ. The etymology is
not certain, although we can hardly
doubt that the word is kindred to the pr.
n. Darius, דָּרְיָוֶשׁ. Others make it either:
a) Dimin. from דריך, daric, δαριήκης, if
the common reading is correct in Strabo
XVI. p. 5874 ; or   b) A compound from
دارا king (Darius) and كون appear-
ance, figure.—The daric was equal in
value to the Attic χρυσοῦς, which, ac-
cording to our mode of reckoning, was
worth nearly 1½ German ducats, or
about three Spanish dollars ; see Boeckh
Staatsh. der Ath. I. p. 23. The coin
usually bears the image of an archer
with a tiara. Darics of gold and silver
are extant in the Museums of Paris and
Vienna. See Eckhel Doctr. Num. P. I.
Vol. III. p. 551.
אַדְרַמֶּלֶךְ (contr. for אֲדַר הַמֶּלֶךְ splen-
dour of the king) Adrammelech, pr. n.
a) An idol of the Sepharvites or Sip-
